quotes.quote: The breadth of inflation narrowed in July, reducing one of the risks the Fed is monitoring. The share of the CPI basket with prices rising 5%+ fell in July and is back to the average levels in 1997-2005, when inflation was close to 2%. This may be the best news in today's report!

The July CPI continued to build the case for disinflation. Core CPI rose 0.2% in July (or annualized 2.6%), firmer than flat prices in June, but still helping to move the trend down. Even so, two months is not enough, and the PPI will also shape whether it's a good PCE print.

Implications for the Fed: good news. Disinflation, even as the Fed's been on hold so far this year, supports its stance. It's too soon to say whether a hold will be appropriate in September—more data coming—but the chances of a hike edged down some today.

There were good details, particularly non-housing core services aka supercore. That's been sticky inflation in recent years and picked up earlier this year. June saw a decline, owing to some outliers. Supercore rose 0.2% in July, which is well below the pace early in the year.

Does the July CPI need to be as soft as the June CPI? No, but it needs to fit the bill of a good CPI. The consensus for core CPI of 0.2% would probably count, though lower is better.

Then the PPI needs to behave too. It's PCE that needs to show disinflation, or a hike is likely.

Put that June core PCE print into the scenarios I built before the release, and it's good news. One month is only one month, but it was real progress on disinflation. 

Keep in mind these are my translations of the minutes. No Fed official would ever be this precise.
